title: Weekly Top Five Articles: Formation Cannot Be Optimized
author: Anthony Bradley
summary: This curated roundup of five articles is united by a single thesis: the formative foundations of personhood require load-bearing commitments that modern culture is systematically dismantling, and neither optimization nor abstraction can replace what is being lost. A CSJ report argues that boys in Britain lack a coherent script for becoming men — the crisis is formational, not primarily economic. Derek Thompson introduces philosopher Agnes Callard's concept of the 'uni-context,' which explains why modernity increasingly sees only what is universal and therefore only what is wrong. A portrait of the rationalist conference Manifest shows what happens when formation via family, religion, and community is abandoned for algorithmic self-improvement. Research across 27 countries links belief in hell (more than heaven) to moral restraint through internalized accountability. A Max Planck study ties declining Finnish church membership to falling birth rates, revealing secularization as a demographic feedback loop that thins the social soil in which belief — and families — remain fruitful.
points: The five articles share a framework: the formative foundations of personhood require load-bearing commitments that modern culture is systematically dismantling, and optimization and abstraction cannot replace what is lost.

The Centre for Social Justice's 'Lost Boys' report argues that boys in Britain are failing not because they lack ambition but because the 'Success Sequence' of education, employment, marriage, and parenthood has been stripped from public culture.

Agnes Callard's concept of the 'uni-context' explains why modernity feels wrong: when all local normative contexts collapse into a single universal frame, only what is universally bad is visible — the good is always local and always the first casualty of abstraction.

A portrait of the Manifest rationalist conference reveals that replacing formation via family, religion, and community with algorithmic self-improvement produces not freedom but a particular kind of loneliness.
Research shows that transcendent belief functions as 'moral scaffolding,' channeling behavior not through external surveillance but through internalized accountability to something beyond the self.
quotes: Five articles, one shared framework: the formative foundations of personhood require load-bearing commitments that our current culture is systematically dismantling, and neither optimization nor abstraction can replace what is being lost.
the crisis is not primarily economic or educational but formational, rooted in the disappearance of fathers, mentors, male spaces, and any credible vision of adulthood worth aspiring to.

a sequence is itself a kind of moral framework, an ordered set of commitments that gives shape to a life from the inside rather than imposing it from the outside. When the sequence is absent, what fills the vacuum is not freedom but drift

goodness is always local, always context-dependent, always requiring patient cultivation in a particular place among particular people, while badness travels universally and requires no interpretation.

the loneliness on display at Manifest is not incidental to the optimization project but is its necessary product: you cannot train a machine-learning model to desire you, because desire is not a function to be optimized but a response to a person whose formation makes him worthy of it.

the fear of transcendent consequences functions as a kind of moral scaffolding, holding behavior in place not through external surveillance but through an internalized sense of accountability to something beyond the self.
faith is never purely individual. It is embedded in a community of shared commitment, and when that community thins, even private conviction loses its generative power.
